title: Emerson's Compensation
hook: every act rewards or punishes itself, Emerson believed (Compensation)

segments.voice: Yesterday, self-reliance, read carefully: are they my poor, and who is the trustee? Your line was self and others. Did your decision hold both? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-nine.

Near the start of the essay, Emerson describes a sermon he disagreed with. He says he heard a preacher explain that in this world things are unjust. The wicked do well, the good suffer, and the balance will be set right later, in the life to come. It's a serious view, with deep roots. Emerson didn't argue about the life to come. What bothered him was the picture of this life, the idea that cheating actually pays here and now, and only gets corrected afterward. His essay answers that the books are balanced sooner than that. He called it Compensation.
screen: `A SERMON HE DISAGREED WITH.` → `THE BALANCE SET RIGHT LATER?` → `THE ESSAY: COMPENSATION.`

segments.voice: First, the big claim, in four words: "Every act rewards itself." Not later. In the act. A deed, as Emerson sees it, carries its own result inside it. Second, his picture from nature. He points to pairs everywhere: light and dark, heat and cold, the tide coming in and going out, breathing in and breathing out. Nothing in nature, he says, comes without its opposite. A gain somewhere means a cost somewhere else. He thought human life worked the same way. Third, the hard line. "Crime and punishment grow out of one stem." The lie and the fear of being found out sprout together. The cheat gets the money and also gets to be a person who cheats, and has to live inside that. And the good act works the same way: the kindness is already doing its work in the one who gave it. Emerson borrows an old Greek saying for this: "The dice of God are always loaded." The game is not random. It's rigged toward balance. Fourth, the honest limit. Emerson can make this sound too neat, as if every life comes out even. Some suffering doesn't look balanced at all. So hold Compensation as a lens, not a guarantee. Some results show up fast. Some take years. Some, you'll have to take on trust. But it's worth watching for, because sometimes the first person an act changes is the one who did it.
screen: `EVERY ACT REWARDS ITSELF.` · `PAIRS EVERYWHERE IN NATURE.` · `ONE STEM, CRIME AND PUNISHMENT.` · `A LENS, NOT A GUARANTEE.` · then, large: `THE DICE OF GOD ARE ALWAYS LOADED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one act's natural result. Settle, and breathe. Bring back something you did in the last day or two. Small is fine. A short temper with someone. A favor done without being asked. A corner cut. A promise kept. Don't judge it. Just follow it forward. What happened next, inside you, or between you and someone else? How did it leave you feeling about yourself? Watch the result grow out of the act, like a plant from its seed. The bell holds the time.
Emerson's Compensation. His essay on the balance in things: every act rewards itself, and crime and punishment grow out of one stem. Today's word.
Your line: it comes back. Before one choice today, ask what it will make of you, not just what it will get you. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Some readers use Emerson's Compensation as a lens for noticing how their actions shape them from the inside, while keeping in mind that he can make life sound more evenly balanced than it is.

notes: Confirm exact wording of the three quotations; 'Every act rewards itself' continues 'or, in other words, integrates itself, in a twofold manner'.

The opening sermon is paraphrased: Emerson says he heard a preacher argue that judgment is not executed in this world, the wicked are successful and the good miserable, with compensation in the next life. The script frames that view respectfully and has Emerson object only to the picture of this life; a Christian reviewer should check the framing.

Emerson's list of pairs in nature is paraphrased; the script's examples (light and dark, heat and cold, ebb and flow, breathing in and out) should be checked against his list (he names darkness and light, heat and cold, ebb and flow of waters, inspiration and expiration, among others).
'His own later essays wrestle with that' points ahead to Experience (day 1205); confirm the fairness of this aside.
The seed image is the narrator's illustration; Emerson's own image here is the one stem.

Editor: the sermon comes near the start, not as the first line (the essay opens with Emerson's boyhood wish to write on compensation); cut the invented 'went home and wrote'; the seed image is no longer attributed to Emerson; cut the unsourced aside about his later essays; fork option adjusted; 'readers often' to 'some readers'.
